analysis.one_liner: Expands Social Security benefits and funds it with payroll taxes on wages above $400,000.
analysis.headline: The Social Security 2100 Act, introduced with 2 cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise Social Security benefits for current and future retirees: a small across-the-board increase, a cost-of-living formula better matched to what seniors actually buy, and a higher minimum benefit for people who worked long careers at low wages. It would also raise more money from the top of the wage scale: all wages above $400,000 would be taxed for Social Security, and the payroll tax rate would rise slowly for everyone, from 6.2% today to 7.2% by 2037. Finally, it would let a new independent board invest up to a quarter of the trust funds in a broad stock index. The bill was sent to three House committees and then to a subcommittee, and nothing more happened before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security beneficiaries. Every beneficiary would get a benefit formula boost, annual cost-of-living adjustments would track an index built for elderly consumers' spending, and lifetime low earners with long work histories would get a minimum benefit of 125% of the poverty line. Middle-income retirees would also keep more of their benefits, since the income thresholds for taxing benefits would rise sharply. Current and future beneficiaries would gain, funded by higher earners.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security beneficiaries, current and future

how_it_helps.text: Raises the benefit formula factor from 90% to 93%, an across-the-board increase for all beneficiaries starting in 2015, with recomputation of existing benefits [S2, S3].
Switches the annual cost-of-living adjustment to the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which reflects the health care and housing costs seniors actually face [S2, S3].
Sets a new special minimum benefit that rises with years worked, reaching 125% of the federal poverty guideline for workers with 30 or more years of work, aimed at lifetime low earners [S2, S3].

Raises the income thresholds at which Social Security benefits become taxable, from $25,000 to $50,000 for single filers and from $32,000 to $100,000 for joint filers, reducing taxes on many middle-income retirees [S2, S3].
Applies the Social Security payroll tax to all wage income above $400,000, closing the gap where high earners stop paying the tax partway through the year [S2, S3].
Reallocates payroll tax revenue toward the disability trust fund, which was approaching depletion at the time [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers and employers would pay gradually higher payroll taxes — the combined employee and employer rate would climb from 12.4% to 14.4% between 2018 and 2037. High earners above $400,000 would pay Social Security tax on their entire wages and self-employment income, including the portion above the current cap, and would get almost nothing back in benefits (only 2% of excess earnings counts in their benefit formula). Employers match the employee tax, so businesses would bear roughly half the rate increase.

drawbacks.text: The payroll tax increase reaches everyone: the rate rises in small annual steps from 6.2% to 7.2% each for employees and employers by 2037, a real cost to working households' paychecks and to employers' payrolls [S2, S3].

Investing up to 25% of the Social Security trust funds in common stock would expose retirement benefits to market downturns; critics of such proposals have long argued that a major market crash could coincide with the trust funds needing to sell stocks to pay benefits. The bill's answer is fiduciary rules, independent oversight, an index-only passive portfolio, and a ban on exercising shareholder voting rights [S3].

The bill raises taxes to expand benefits rather than cutting them, so it does not reduce the deficit and the tax increases begin immediately while some benefit improvements phase in over years [S2, S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is broad and well-targeted: it lifts the floor for lifetime low earners, fixes a cost-of-living measure that understates seniors' costs, and untaxes more middle-income retirees. The costs are a real but gradual payroll tax increase, falling hardest on high earners above $400,000 who would pay on income now exempt. The boldest design choice — stock investment of trust funds — is hedged with strict passive-index and fiduciary rules, but it is still the part most likely to draw fair criticism. On balance this is a conventional expand-and-fund package whose main weakness is political, not technical: it asked the members with the most power to move it to take a vote, and they never did.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees and then to a subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. John Larson introduced the bill on July 31, 2014 [S1, S3, S5].
It was referred to the Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, and Budget committees on the day of introduction [S1, S5].
On November 17, 2014 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions, and no further action appears in the record [S5].
The bill ended with just 2 cosponsors, both Democrats [S4].
No vote was ever taken in either chamber before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners above the $400,000 mark and employers kept their existing payroll tax exposure, while Social Security beneficiaries gained nothing from the proposed benefit increases. The committee chairs with jurisdiction never had to take a position on the record.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners, employers, and committee chairs

for.name: Rep. John B. Larson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Social Security 2100 Act on July 31, 2014.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee with jurisdiction over Social Security legislation in the 113th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after its referral in July 2014; the record shows no committee action beyond a subcommittee referral in November 2014.

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls were ever taken, so no voting split exists; the only recorded support was Democratic — the sponsor and 2 Democratic cosponsors, with no Republican cosponsors [S4].

industries.industry: High earners above the $400,000 wage cap
industries.note: They would pay the 12.4% payroll tax on all wage and self-employment income above $400,000, income currently exempt, while only 2% of those excess earnings counts toward their benefits. Avoiding the bill preserved that arrangement.
Employers match the employee Social Security tax, so the scheduled rise from 6.2% to 7.2% by 2037 would have raised their cost of employing workers. Blocking the bill avoided that cost.

industries.industry: Low-cost index fund and asset management firms
industries.note: The bill would have created stock investment funds inside the Social Security trust funds, up to 25% of assets, invested passively in a broad market index under fiduciary rules. That would be a very large, very cheap new client for index managers, though the bill bans voting rights and requires low administrative costs.
